channel.title: TENMAY — Notes from the PCBA line
channel.description: Process limits, quoting arithmetic and BOM problems, written from a high-mix PCBA floor in Shenzhen.

item.title: Who owns the optics on a dashcam build?
item.description: The sensor board is assembled and the lens focused by different suppliers. Get the boundary wrong and the camera is sharp on the bench only.

item.title: Should you buy the e-bike controller and display from one assembler?
item.description: Splitting the controller and the display across two assemblers is often right. What it costs is a harness nobody owns, unless you write the drawing yourself.

item.title: What an EVSE control board audit actually asks for
item.description: On a charging point the certification depends on the build being repeatable, so the audit asks for records rather than capability. Here is the file to demand.

item.title: Buy a certified HMI module, or assemble the board yourself?
item.description: A module arrives with its isolation certified; a bare board leaves the barrier to you. The choice decides who answers for a field fault.

item.title: Where liability sits on a jump starter with an air compressor
item.description: Two boards, a high-current switch, a compressor motor. The assembly is simple; what needs agreeing is who certifies what before a battery is connected.

item.title: How to tell whether an LED driver PCBA quote is real
item.description: This is the most price-compressed family there is. Five line items separate a quote that holds for a year from one that gets re-priced at the second batch.

item.title: Potting before test turns a defect into scrap
item.description: On a small potted board, the order of the last two steps decides the scrap rate. Once the compound cures, nothing inside is inspectable or reworkable.

item.title: Should one assembler build all three portable power station boards?
item.description: The BMS, the inverter and the display fail for different reasons but share one battery and one certificate file. What to keep together, what to split.

item.title: Do you actually need in-circuit test on a robot vacuum mainboard?
item.description: ICT quietly decides which assemblers can quote a robot vacuum at all. Here is what it proves, what it misses, and how to specify it honestly.

item.title: Sharing a build stack between servo drives and VFDs
item.description: Servo drives and VFDs share a power stage, not a market. Consolidating them at one assembler is leverage until it becomes a single point of failure.

item.title: The 800 mm board is not the hard part of a treadmill build
item.description: Motor drive, console and a board at the largest panel size carried. The placement is routine; field failures come from connectors and heat, not solder.

item.title: Quoting a VFD as three boards or as one set
item.description: A drive is a control board, a power board and a keypad. Quoting them as separate lines and as one set answer different questions, and buyers usually need both.

item.title: Consigned vs turnkey PCBA at 50, 500 and 5,000 pieces
item.description: Where the three real costs sit when you consign components instead of buying turnkey, what changes at 50, 500 and 5,000 pieces, and which model wins.

item.title: 01005 vs 0201: which package should your design use?
item.description: 01005 is 0.4 x 0.2 mm and 0201 is 0.6 x 0.3 mm. The larger part is cheaper and yields better; here is when the smaller one is actually necessary.

item.title: What SPI, AOI and X-ray can catch — and what they cannot
item.description: In-line inspection catches placement and joint defects, not electrical ones. What each station proves, what passes through it, and what still needs a test.

item.title: What is HMLV in PCBA — and when does it cost more than high volume?
item.description: HMLV means high-mix, low-volume PCBA: many part numbers, small batches each. What it changes, when it costs more than volume builds, and when it does not.

item.title: What actually limits 01005 placement yield?
item.description: 01005 passives fail for reasons that have nothing to do with the placement head. Stencil aperture, paste type, pad geometry and inspection each set a ceiling.

item.title: Which BOM problems force a re-quote — and how do you catch them first?
item.description: A BOM can be complete and still unbuyable. Eight checks on lifecycle, alternates, ratings, MSL, packaging and MOQ decide whether parts arrive as listed.

item.title: Why does a 50-piece PCBA run cost more per board than 5,000?
item.description: Setup, stencil, programming and first-article work do not change with batch size. Here is where the money goes on a small run, and which parts of the gap are not real.
